workingTitle: A cold giant planet challenges the usual growth route
publicationStatus: Accepted and in press at The Astrophysical Journal Letters; arXiv version submitted November 11, 2026
coreFacts: Forty-seven Planet Finder Spectrograph observing epochs across 41 nights from 2010 to 2025 reveal the star's long-period radial-velocity wobble.
The preferred orbital period is about 7,055 days, or 19.3 years, and the radial-velocity semiamplitude is 94.9 metres per second.
Combining the radial velocities with Hipparcos and Gaia astrometry gives HIP 88962 b a true mass of 4.83 Jupiter masses, a semimajor axis of 6.15 astronomical units, and eccentricity 0.718.
The host is a K7V dwarf about 27.3 parsecs away with an adopted mass of 0.62 solar masses.

Published core-accretion population models do not produce a planet this massive this far from such a low-mass star, while gas-disk gravitational instability can; formation by disk instability is an interpretation, not a direct observation.
A possible 4.11-day residual signal is not considered a robust second planet because stellar activity can account for the remaining scatter.

sources.label: Boss et al., accepted by The Astrophysical Journal Letters

sourceStatus: Full accepted manuscript and arXiv metadata read; observation count, orbital solution, host properties, formation argument, and residual-signal caveat checked.
caveats: The accepted manuscript is available as an arXiv preprint; the journal version is still in press.
The disk-instability origin is inferred by comparison with published formation models, not directly observed.
Limited orbital coverage allows alternative long-period fits, so continued radial-velocity monitoring is needed.
The 4.11-day residual is not a robust second-planet detection.
